questions.q: Define verbal irony and give one example from everyday Hindi conversation (not from the textbook).
questions.a: Verbal irony occurs when a speaker says something but means the opposite, often for critique or humor. Example: A student arriving late to class hears the teacher say, "बहुत जल्दी आ गए आप!" (You've arrived very early!). A wrong answer that merely defines irony as "saying the opposite" without the element of intentional contrast or context reveals the student confuses irony with simple negation or lying.

questions.q: In Dajju's verse where he calls the body a "cage" (पिंजरा) and the soul a "bird" (टिटिहरी/पक्षी), explain why this is symbolism and not just a metaphor. Use the distinction between the two devices.
questions.a: Symbolism operates across the whole work — the bird/cage image recurs and carries the weight of the soul's entrapment in matter, becoming a standing emblem for the human condition. A metaphor is a localized comparison ("life is a journey"). If the student says "both compare two things," they miss that a symbol functions as a persistent, multi-layered signifier woven into the poem's architecture, not a single decorative comparison.

questions.q: Read these two lines from the chapter: "कहत कबीर सुनो भई साधो, सबही खाल की श्वास" and "पोथी पढ़ि पढ़ि जग मुआ, पंडित भया न कोय". Identify the TYPE of irony in each line and justify your classification in one sentence per line.
questions.a: First line: verbal irony — Kabir addresses "holy ones" (साधो) while implying they are far from saintly. Second line: situational irony — the expected outcome (reading scriptures makes one wise) is reversed (the reader dies unenlightened). A wrong answer labeling both as "verbal irony" shows the student cannot distinguish between irony residing in spoken words versus irony residing in the situation's outcome.

questions.q: Compare the symbol of the "bird" (टिटिहरी/पक्षी) in Dajju's poetry with the symbol of the "caged bird" in Maya Angelou's poem "Caged Bird". How does the cultural context shift the symbolic meaning even though the core image is similar?
questions.a: Dajju's bird represents the individual soul (जीवात्मा) yearning for union with the Divine (परमात्मा) — a spiritual liberation from the cycle of birth-death. Angelou's bird symbolizes the African-American struggle against racial oppression — a socio-political liberation. The student who writes "both mean freedom" misses that symbols are culturally coded; the same image carries different freight depending on the belief system and historical moment it emerges from.

questions.q: Critique this student statement: "Dajju uses irony only to mock priests and pandits; it has no positive spiritual function." Defend or refute using evidence from the verses.
questions.a: Refute. Dajju's irony clears false paths so the true path (नाम-स्मरण, गुरु-भक्ति) can shine. Example: mocking external rituals ("माला फेरत जुग भया") creates a vacuum that the positive teaching ("मन का मनका फेर") fills. A student who agrees with the statement sees irony as purely destructive, missing its constructive role in nirguna bhakti — it is a surgical tool, not a sledgehammer.

questions.q: Compose a four-line Hindi couplet (दोहा) that uses BOTH irony and a symbol to convey a message about modern education (e.g., degrees vs. wisdom, coaching vs. understanding). Label which line carries irony and which image is the symbol.
questions.a: Sample: "डिग्री सजे दीवार पे, ज्ञान रहा बेचार / कोचिंग के पिंजरे में, उड़ न पाया सार" — Irony in line 1 (degree displayed but wisdom absent); Symbol: "पिंजरा" (coaching centre as cage trapping the bird of true understanding). A poor answer uses irony and symbol as decoration without integrating them into a coherent critique, showing the student treats devices as ornaments rather than meaning-making tools.
